subject: 7D483E56354A41E7BBF405202EC78AAE
introduction: “If the eyelid, however delicate, can deprive man’s outer eye from beholding the world … consider then what would be wrought if the veil of covetousness were to descend upon his inner eye.” The readings treat greed and envy first as a blindness, then as a fire that consumes persons, families and nations, and finally as something mortality exposes; contentment and detachment are the cure. The Bible’s witnesses are many: the tenth commandment, Ahab sick with wanting a vineyard, Cain, Joseph’s brothers, the rich fool, the young man with great possessions, “the love of money is the root of all evil”, James on where wars come from. The Qur’an’s “rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you until ye come to the graves” and the Dhammapada’s thirst that “grows like a creeper” agree. Wordsworth and Emerson said it for the industrial age. Two voices complicate the picture. Adam Smith observed that dinner comes from the tradesman’s self-interest, not his benevolence, and reading 30 itself grants that such thoughts make the world prosper. Mencius, against reading 23, held that human nature tends to good.
questions: The readings call covetousness a veil over the inner eye. What, concretely, does a covetous person fail to see?
Reading 3 contrasts a rich man who was detached with a poor man attached to his donkey. What then is the test of attachment, if it is not how much one owns?

Adam Smith says we owe our dinner to the baker’s self-interest; reading 30 says thoughts of wealth were given “so that this world might prosper”. How do the readings distinguish useful ambition from greed?
Reading 32 says jealousy alone has no cure. Emerson says the cure is to “take himself … as his portion”. Who is right, in your observation?
Why do so many of these texts answer greed by pointing to death?

outside.why: If an eyelid can hide the world, what of the veil of covetousness on the inner eye? If thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness.
The last of the commandments forbids not an act but a looking: thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s.
Let not the heart, love’s habitation, be destroyed by covetous desires. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

A rich man who had reached sacrifice, and a poor one attached to his donkey. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God; the story adds that it is not the amount.
Some dream that with ten thousand dollars they would be happy. He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase.
Rich men as wood-carriers of their own wealth. Emerson: the merchant serves the purse; things are in the saddle, and ride mankind.
Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
He would kill one who looks at his house; soon his enemies will have it. Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
Consumed night and day by the fire of greed. Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you, until ye come to the graves.
A king with three hundred and sixty palaces. Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair! Nothing beside remains.
The Preacher, who says he had it all: vanity of vanities; all is vanity. What profit hath a man of all his labour?
Every treasure has been a cause of grief. Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal.
War and strife come from greed and avarice. From whence come wars and fightings among you? Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain.
Their wealth comes from the efforts of the poor. The hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth.

Adam Smith built an account of prosperity on the motive the readings condemn: it is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. Is self-interest in trade the same thing as the greed of these readings? Where would you draw the line?

A few spans of earth blind men to justice. Ahab the king wanted a neighbour’s vineyard for a herb garden, was refused, and lay down on his bed and would eat no bread; the neighbour was dead within the chapter.
Greed burned away spiritual qualities, and envy was kindled in its place. A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.
A brother’s envy, after every kindness. The Lord to Cain: why art thou wroth? If thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door.
Souls who cling to evil from greed alone. The love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
The serpent means attachment to the material world. The woman saw that the tree was good for food, and pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired.
All are fettered by self and desire. The Dhammapada: the thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper.
A prisoner of wealth one day, of fame the next. No man can serve two masters. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
People give their lives for the sake of dust. For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?

“Greed and avarice are ingrained in human nature.” Mencius held the opposite about nature: the tendency of man’s nature to good is like the tendency of water to flow downwards. If greed is ingrained, what is the education the readings hope for working on?
Desire is a flame that has burned the harvests of the learned. Wordsworth: getting and spending, we lay waste our powers; we have given our hearts away, a sordid boon.
Clergy who pray all day and are held back by attachment. The Qur’an says a like thing of rabbis and monks who devour the wealth of mankind, and of all who hoard up gold and silver.
Covetousness has stopped your ears. The invited guests: I have bought a piece of ground; I have bought five yoke of oxen; I pray thee have me excused.
“God is in this box.” The young man went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.
Had the world any worth in His sight, He would not have left it to His enemies. The life of the world is only play, and idle talk, and pageantry, and rivalry in respect of wealth and children.

Thoughts of wealth and rank are illusion, planted so that the world might prosper. The Preacher saw the same engine and gave no reason for it: I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. If ambition and rivalry build the world, how far should they be cured?

Envy makes a short life miserable. Emerson: there is a time in every man’s education when he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance; that he must take himself for better, for worse, as his portion.
Jealousy is the one disease without a cure. Milton’s Satan, whose fall begins in envy, is the portrait: better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.
Practise contentment in all conditions. Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
A heart with the least remnant of envy shall not attain. Of Joseph’s dreams: and his brethren envied him.
One who covets the property of others is not of the people of Bahá. Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have.
Blessed is the soul that has cast off the garment of greed. Consider the lilies of the field: even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
Abandon what you possess; nothing shall profit you this day. Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither.
People wish to remain here always, like a bird in a cage. Blake: how can the bird that is born for joy sit in a cage and sing?

shortfall: Readings 5, 15, 16 and 27 to 28 concern particular persons in the community’s history, and 19 to 22 repeat one sentence about universal greed; these were given few companions, and the count is below the guide’s for that reason.

kings-naboths-vineyard.text: And Ahab spake unto Naboth, saying, Give me thy vineyard, that I may have it for a garden of herbs, because it is near unto my house: and I will give thee for it a better vineyard than it; or, if it seem good to thee, I will give thee the worth of it in money. And Naboth said to Ahab, The Lord forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee. And Ahab came into his house heavy and displeased because of the word which Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him: for he had said, I will not give thee the inheritance of my fathers. And he laid him down upon his bed, and turned away his face, and would eat no bread

ecclesiastes-envied-of-his-neighbour.text: Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This is also vanity and vexation of spirit
